items.name: 250 mL beaker
items.summary: A 250 mL glass beaker for holding, mixing and heating liquids. Its marks are only approximate.
safeUse: Carry it with one hand under the base, not by the rim.
When you heat it, fill it to 150 mL at most, so it cannot boil over.
Heat it on a hot plate or on a gauze over a tripod, never straight in a flame.
Use a measuring cylinder or pipette when the volume matters.
Let hot glass cool before you touch it: hot glass looks the same as cold glass.

mistakes.when: The hot plate is on and the beaker is empty.
mistakes.say: The beaker is empty on a hot plate: heating dry glass can crack it. Turn the plate off.

mistakes.when: The hot plate is on with more than 150 mL in the beaker.
mistakes.say: That is too full to heat: it can boil over. Pour some out first.

mistakes.when: The beaker holds more than its 250 mL mark.
mistakes.say: The beaker is filled past 250 mL: it will spill when you carry it.

hazards: Hot glass and hot liquid can burn.
Chipped or cracked glass can cut and can break when heated.
Some solutions (copper sulfate, potassium permanganate) are harmful: wear goggles and gloves.

liquid.how: The liquid is a lathe of the inner profile from the floor to levelMm[volume]; scale its node along up from the floor, or rebuild it

items.name: Bench power supply
items.summary: A 0-30 V, 0-5 A bench supply. It holds the voltage you set (CV) until the load wants more than the current limit, then it holds the current (CC).
safeUse: Turn the output off before you connect or change anything.
Set the voltage first, then set the current limit a little above what your circuit should draw.
Use red for + and black for -; green is mains earth, not the negative output.
If the CC lamp lights when you did not expect it, something draws too much: turn off and check the circuit.
Never short the output with the current limit turned up.

mistakes.when: The output is on into a short with the current limit above 1 A.
mistakes.say: That is a short with the current limit turned up. Turn the output off and turn the current limit down.

mistakes.when: The resistor on the output burns more power than its rating.
mistakes.say: The resistor is burning more than its rating and will overheat. Lower the voltage or use a bigger resistor.

mistakes.when: The output is on into a load with the current limit at the 5 A maximum.
mistakes.say: The current limit is at maximum, so it protects nothing. Set it just above what the circuit needs.

hazards: A short or a wrong connection can burn parts and wires.
Overloaded resistors get hot enough to burn fingers.
The mains inside the case is dangerous: never open it while plugged in.

items.name: Bunsen burner
items.summary: A gas burner. The air collar sets the flame: closed gives a yellow safety flame, open gives a hot roaring blue flame.
safeUse: Tie back long hair, wear goggles, and stand the burner on a heat-proof mat away from paper.
Close the air collar before you light it.
Have the lit splint or lighter ready over the barrel before you turn the gas on, then light it at once.
Open the collar for a hot blue flame only while you are heating something.
When you are not heating, close the collar to the yellow safety flame so everyone can see it.
Turn the gas off at the tap when you finish.
For a flame test, hold the clean loop at the edge of a blue flame, not in the yellow safety flame.

mistakes.when: The gas tap has been on for more than 2 seconds with no flame.
mistakes.say: Gas is on but not lit. Turn the gas tap off now, then light it the right way.

mistakes.when: Someone tried to light it with the air collar open, and the gas is still on.
mistakes.say: It will not light with the collar open. Turn the gas off, close the collar, then try again.

mistakes.when: A roaring blue flame has burned for over 20 seconds with nothing being heated in it.
mistakes.say: A blue flame is hard to see. If you are not heating, close the collar to the yellow safety flame.

mistakes.when: A flame-test sample is held in the yellow luminous flame (air collar closed).
mistakes.say: The yellow flame hides the test colour. Open the air collar to a blue flame, then look again.

hazards: Unburnt gas can build up and explode.
A blue flame is almost invisible in daylight.
The barrel stays hot after the flame is out.
Hair, sleeves and paper catch fire.

flameTest.how: Tint the flame channel with colors[sample].hex while tintWhen holds; the inner cone stays blue

items.name: Digital balance
items.summary: A balance that weighs to 0.01 g. TARE sets the zero, so put the empty boat on, press TARE, then add the sample.
safeUse: Stand it level, on a steady bench away from draughts.
Put the empty weighing boat on the pan and press TARE before you add the sample.
Add the sample with a spatula, off to the side of the balance, not over it.
Wait for the reading to settle before you write it down.
Never put anything hot, wet or heavier than 400 g on the pan.

mistakes.when: The sample is weighed in the boat without the empty boat having been tared.
mistakes.say: You did not tare the empty boat, so the reading includes the boat. Take the sample out, tare the empty boat, then weigh again.

mistakes.when: TARE was pressed with the sample already in the boat.
mistakes.say: You pressed TARE with the sample in the boat, so it reads zero. Tare the empty boat, then add the sample.

hazards: Spilt chemicals on the pan corrode it and spoil later readings.

extras.readout: report.readingG to 2 decimals and "g"; "NET" while report.net

items.name: 250 mL conical flask
items.summary: A 250 mL conical (Erlenmeyer) flask for mixing, swirling and titrations. Its sloping sides keep the liquid in when you swirl it.
safeUse: Swirl it by moving your wrist in small circles, holding the neck.
Keep it to 150 mL or less when you swirl it, so nothing climbs out.
Stand it on a white tile under a burette to see a colour change.
Never heat it with a stopper in: the pressure can burst it.

mistakes.when: The flask is swirled with more than 150 mL in it.
mistakes.say: That flask is too full to swirl: keep it under about half full or it will slop out.

mistakes.when: The flask holds more than its 250 mL mark.
mistakes.say: The flask is filled past 250 mL: there is no room left to mix.

hazards: Glass breaks and cuts.
A stoppered flask can burst when heated.
Some solutions are harmful: wear goggles.

liquid.how: The liquid is a lathe of the inner profile from the floor to levelMm[volume]; rebuild it, since the cone is not a straight scale

items.name: Flame test kit
items.summary: A wire loop, seven known metal chlorides, one unknown and dilute acid. A clean loop dipped in a salt and held in a blue flame colours the flame by the metal.
safeUse: Wear goggles: the acid and some of the salts are harmful, and barium and copper salts are toxic.
Clean the loop first: dip it in the acid, then hold it in a blue flame until it adds no colour.
Clean it again between every two salts.
Hold the loop at the edge of a blue flame, not in the yellow safety flame.
Look at the first flash of colour: compare it with the known salts before you name the unknown.
Rest the loop on its stand so the hot wire does not touch the bench.

mistakes.when: The loop touched a salt before it was ever cleaned in the acid.
mistakes.say: The loop was not cleaned first, so it carries sodium from your fingers. Clean it in the acid and the flame, then dip again.

mistakes.when: The loop was dipped in a second salt without cleaning it after the first one.
mistakes.say: The loop still carries the last salt, so the colour will be mixed, and sodium yellow hides the others. Clean it first.

hazards: Hydrochloric acid irritates skin and eyes.
Barium and copper salts are toxic if swallowed.
The wire stays hot after the flame.
Long hair and sleeves near the flame catch fire.

carry.label: Left on the loop from before

loop.bead: colour the loop tip with saltColor[report.sample] while params.salt is set; bare wire when it is null

extras.toBurner: pass report.sample to bunsen-burner as its sample param while the loop is held in the flame

items.name: Function generator
items.summary: A function generator makes a test signal: a sine, square or triangle wave at the frequency and size you set, from its 50 Ω OUT socket.
safeUse: Set the waveform, frequency and amplitude with the output off, then turn the output on.
Start with a small amplitude, about 1 to 2 V peak-to-peak, and turn it up only as far as you need.
Connect the black (outer) lead to the circuit ground.
Never let the output leads touch each other while the output is on.
Turn the output off before you change the connections.

mistakes.when: The output is on and its clips touch each other (a short).
mistakes.say: The output is shorted: the clips are touching. Turn the output off, then separate the clips.

mistakes.when: The output is on into the oscilloscope with the amplitude at its 20 V maximum.
mistakes.say: That is the maximum amplitude, much more than you need. Turn it down to a few volts before it overdrives the circuit or the scope.

hazards: A shorted output heats the generator's output stage.
Twenty volts peak-to-peak can damage small parts and logic inputs.

extras.toScope: report.signal is the oscilloscope demo signal: send it as { source: "demo", ...signal }

items.name: Oscilloscope
items.summary: A 2-channel oscilloscope. It draws voltage against time: up is volts (VOLTS/DIV per square), across is time (TIME/DIV per square).
safeUse: Set the probe switch and the channel probe setting the same: both ×10 for normal work.
Check the probe on the CAL lug first: you should see a flat-topped 1 kHz square wave.
Clip the probe ground lead to the circuit ground only, never to any other point.
Turn VOLTS/DIV until the trace fills most of the screen without running off it.
Turn TIME/DIV until you see one to five cycles.
Never probe mains with a bench scope and a standard probe.

mistakes.when: The probe switch and the channel probe setting differ (×10 probe with the channel on ×1, or the other way).
mistakes.say: The probe switch and the channel setting do not match, so every reading is ten times wrong. Set both to ×10.

mistakes.when: The trace runs off the top or bottom of the screen at this VOLTS/DIV.
mistakes.say: The trace runs off the screen. Turn VOLTS/DIV up to a bigger number so the whole wave fits.

mistakes.when: The whole trace is less than one division tall.
mistakes.say: The trace is tiny. Turn VOLTS/DIV down so the wave fills more of the screen.

mistakes.when: Fewer than 1 or more than 5 cycles fit across the screen at this TIME/DIV.
mistakes.say: TIME/DIV is off: you cannot see whole cycles clearly. Turn it until one to five cycles fit across.

hazards: The probe ground is connected to mains earth: clipping it to a live point makes a short.
High voltages can damage the scope and hurt you.

screen.trace: y(t) = g·(offset + vpp/2·wave(f·t + phase)) in divisions of vdiv, t in divisions of timebase, trigger point at the centre; g = atten ÷ probe

extras.signalFrom: a function-generator report.signal can be sent as { source: "demo", wave, freqHz, vpp, offset }

items.name: Simple pendulum
items.summary: A simple pendulum on a retort stand. Its period depends on the string length, T = 2π√(L/g), not on the mass of the bob.
safeUse: Clamp the stand to the bench, or put a heavy weight on its base, so it cannot tip.
Measure L from the pivot to the centre of the bob.
Release the bob from a small angle, under about 15 degrees, without pushing it.
Time 10 swings and divide by 10: it is much more accurate than timing one.
Start the timer as the bob passes the lowest point, where it moves fastest.

mistakes.when: The bob is swinging from a release angle above 15 degrees.
mistakes.say: That swing is too big for the formula: release it from under about 15 degrees.

hazards: A tall stand can tip over: keep the clamp over the base.
A heavy swinging bob can hit faces and glassware.

extras.angle: amplitude * cos(2π t / report.periodS) while swinging

items.name: pH meter
items.summary: A pH meter reads how acidic or alkaline a liquid is from a glass electrode. It must be calibrated with buffers first, and the electrode rinsed between liquids.
safeUse: Calibrate it before you measure: pH 7 buffer first, then 4, then 10.
Rinse the electrode with distilled water between every two liquids, and dab it dry with a tissue; never wipe the bulb.
Dip the bulb fully and wait for the reading to settle.
Never let the bulb touch the bottom or sides of the beaker: the glass is thin.
When you finish, rinse it and put the storage cap back on.
Wear goggles with acids and alkalis.

mistakes.when: The electrode went from one liquid into the next without being rinsed.
mistakes.say: The electrode was not rinsed, so the last liquid is spoiling this reading. Rinse it with distilled water first.

mistakes.when: A sample (water, acid or alkali) is being measured before the meter was calibrated.
mistakes.say: The meter is not calibrated, so this reading can be a whole unit out. Calibrate it with the pH 7, 4 and 10 buffers first.

mistakes.when: The electrode has been out of any liquid and out of its storage cap for over 10 seconds.
mistakes.say: The electrode is drying out in the air, which spoils the glass bulb. Put its storage cap back on.

hazards: Acids and alkalis harm skin and eyes.
The glass bulb breaks easily and can cut.

extras.readout: report.readingPH to 2 decimals and 25.0 °C; "-.--" when null

items.name: Soldering station
items.summary: A temperature-controlled soldering iron. The tip runs at the dial temperature, about 330 °C for normal work, and looks the same hot or cold.
safeUse: Always put the iron back in its stand, never down on the bench.
Hold it by the grip only; never touch the metal.
Use about 320 to 350 °C for normal through-hole soldering.
Keep the sponge damp, not wet, and wipe the tip on it before each joint.
Work with a fan or fume extractor so you do not breathe the flux smoke.
Switch it off when you finish or walk away.

mistakes.when: The station is on and the iron has been out of its stand for over 15 seconds.
mistakes.say: Put the iron back in its stand when you are not soldering: a hot iron on the bench burns things.

mistakes.when: The station is on with the dial at 400 °C or more.
mistakes.say: That is hotter than you need. Around 330 °C is enough; hotter burns the tip and can lift the pads.

mistakes.when: The station is on with a dry sponge.
mistakes.say: Dampen the sponge first: a dry one melts and does not clean the tip.

hazards: The tip is around 330 °C and looks cold.
Flux smoke irritates the lungs.
Solder can spit: wear safety glasses.
